prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene fits the mandate as I read it: a discovery experimentally verified, with an original experiment behind it. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, and the Jarillo-Herrero group then observed correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Transport was followed by scanning-probe and spectroscopic imaging from many independent groups, and the same physics was reproduced in twisted multilayers and moire TMD systems within a few years. It is a door-opening platform in the sense I value: a tunable knob (twist angle, gating) that gives access to correlated phases nobody could previously dial in a simple carbon system. It also has the broadest opening support among the experimental condensed-matter entries (five of eight members have it in their top three, six rank it, and every other ranking member places it between second and fourth), which suggests the committee is already converging on it. The theory-plus-experiment trio is a clean allocation from the supplied names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing and attribution. The discovery is under a decade old, the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and sample-to-sample variation from strain and disorder is large, so a cautious reading says wait. On attribution, the first author of the 2018 experimental papers (Yuan Cao) is not creditable under the supplied names, and earlier continuum-model work (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Suarez Morell and colleagues) may carry priority claims on parts of the flat-band picture. If the historical record shows the decisive experimental credit is more diffuse than one group leader, the configuration is weaker than it looks. I want to be absolutely sure the people credited did the original work before I settle on this.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a measurement instrument in the strict sense, with 1e-18 uncertainty, reproduced by several laboratories, and a clean two-person credit (Katori, Ye) that enables geodesy, tests of constants and a route to redefining the second.
responses.response: I agree that B061 is the most robust candidate on reproducibility and attribution, and I ranked it third for that reason; it is why I name it as my first alternative. Where I differ is on novelty. The comb (2005) and the ion clock (2012) prizes already honoured the enabling techniques, and the lattice clock is in significant part a refinement along that line, even if the magic-wavelength idea is original. B013 opened a regime nobody could previously reach, whereas B061 extends one that was already open. I would not object strongly to B061 if the committee puts weight on its clean record and universal ranking, but I want the citation to name the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation, not the precision figure alone.

responses.point: Mehlig puts the geometric-phase entry (Aharonov, Berry) first, as a clean universal mechanism underlying Hall quantisation and topological band theory, and notes B013 is likely on the early side though very strong.
responses.response: I accept that the mechanism-first argument is compelling, and B008 is mature. My difficulty is the committee's rule that the prize is for an original, experimentally verified discovery. The Aharonov-Bohm effect has a deceased co-originator in Bohm, and Berry's phase has acknowledged precursors (Pancharatnam), so the credit story is far less clean than he suggests, and only Lindroth shares his ranking. I agree with his point that B013 is early. I weigh that against the fact that the central phenomena have been reproduced across platforms, and that the superconducting mechanism affects the interpretation but not the discovery. He is right that priority of earlier theory in B013 needs a historical check, and I would want that done before the final ballot.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks time-reversal-invariant topological insulators first, as a new organising principle of band insulators with protected edge states, and flags that HgTe-prediction credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 3D work fall outside the credited names.
responses.response: I share his assessment of the science and ranked B019 fourth, and I think it is a serious alternative. But his own attribution caveat is, to my mind, the decisive weakness. The Kane-Mele proposal, the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (Zhang is deceased), and the Molenkamp experiment are three different steps, and the 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan, Cava, Shen and others) are a separate line. A three-name set leaves out major contributors, and the 2016 prize already covers topological phases. B013 has a more compact discovery chain, and that is why I place it ahead. If the committee can agree on a narrowly defined citation for the QSH effect, I would support it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first as an instrument built to find a flux it then found, with the diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 results, crediting Halzen and Spiering as the instigators.
responses.response: I ranked B009 sixth and I take his point that this is a new messenger opening a window, which is the sort of tool I like. My concern is the 'original experiment' test. The diffuse flux is secure, but source identifications remain at modest significance, and the founding credit is spread across DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA. Naming two people for a collaboration of hundreds is a judgement about instigators rather than the original experiment. I would want the committee to establish clearly who made the first detection, as distinct from who led the programme, before I could support it.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record on the flat-band picture and the 2018 experiments supports crediting only these three names, given earlier theoretical work and the uncredited first author.
Whether the committee regards the discovery as mature enough while the pairing mechanism is unresolved.
Whether the novelty of the lattice clock over the 2005 and 2012 prizes is large enough that B061 outranks B013 for the committee as a whole.
Whether the compound B019 credit chain can be narrowed to a fair three-person set.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile with any shortlisted candidate or credited person. My profile notes a colleague on this committee (Johansson) is also at Chalmers Physics, and I have worked with Tohoku and Tokyo microscopy communities; Katori is Japanese, but I have no known personal or institutional tie to him. I would raise any connection if it surfaced.
